utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We also take note of your comments. Yes, we've got the point, Mr. Kovacic. No need to belabour the point. Mr. Praljak said, "Yes, I took part in the meeting," but he does not understand the meaning of these excerpts that are being produced. What would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to say, but Your Honour has already asked the witness. We don't know what the provenance of this document is, so there is no foundation for this document, and it's being used if examination. We don't know what the value of the document is. What is it, in fact? The witness is evaluating this document but no foundation has been laid. Where does this document come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, we have a handwritten document here. Where does that document come from? I assume it's a document that was found by the investigators of the OTP somewhere. Can you provide us some explanations about this, because the excerpts in English are excerpts of some paragraphs of the document, and I suppose that in B/C/S we might have only excerpts of the document. So is there another larger document, more comprehensive?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, without doing a specific check at this time I would have to -- my answer would be this, subject to verification: It is either -- it comes either from the operational log of the Central Bosnia -- the HVO Central Bosnia Operative Zone of which Tihomir Blaskic was the zone commander, or it comes from -- it may come from, as counsel suggested, it may come from his -- from his own personal logbook. Those are the two sources that I'm -- would be most familiar with. I can certainly check that further. I do note that it has the stamp of the HVO Croatian State Archive or, excuse me, the Croatian State Archive in the upper right portion of the page. It is by all indications part of a longer document. Mr. President, once again, if the Chamber -- the Chamber is always coming in and saying I have this avalanche of documents. If the Chamber wants another 200 pages to go with this particular two pages, we can -- three or four pages we can happily do that. There comes a time -- let me just suggest, and I'm in the Chamber's hands, of course, but it seems to me there comes a time where there has to be, for some representation, that the document comes from a much larger document and we have to go forward on that basis, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but by tomorrow you will be able to tell us where that document comes from. You're assuming, and you might be right, that this document might come from the personal archives of Colonel Blaskic, and it might even be Colonel Blaskic's handwriting we have here. He might be the one who drafted this document. This is just an assumption, and there might be other assumptions, but I believe by tomorrow you might be able to know where the document comes from because we have a written document with a stamp, yes, of course, but we don't know exactly where the document comes from. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for taking up time, but I think we have now reached the crux of the matter. First of all, I suggest that the witness be asked about the provenance of the document, but also because I know what document this is, regardless of what the witness knows. I have to say that as my colleague said, as my learned friend said, it's a document from the operative zone, but it's Blaskic's personal diary, and in the Blaskic appeal this same OTP claims that the document is not authentic, that Blaskic wrote it up later, subsequently, after all of these events while preparing for his testimony before this Tribunal. That's what the Prosecutor claims in the Blaskic appeal. So in the appeal they say this is a non-authentic document which Blaskic prepared for his defence, but in this case the expert witness is dealing with the document. He hasn't told us what the document is. This is being evaded, and I wanted the witness to be asked this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've heard our discussion. You've had access to this document because you've probably -- most probably read it whilst preparing your report. Did you know where that document came from? Is this a document produced by Colonel Blaskic, a document he drafted himself? And apparently, some said that although this document is dated 2nd of April, 1993, apparently, according to some, this document could have been drafted later in the preparation of his case. What do you have to answer to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll begin at the very start. This particular document was found in the Croatian state archives, I believe late in the year 2000 by our investigators. It bears on the upper right-hand corner, you can see right now that's -- it's displayed, the stamp of the Croatian archives. I believe it was discovered along with other documents of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia. What the Defence counsel was talking about is an issue having to do with previous trials as to how these particular documents would have been characterised, either as personal diaries or unit diaries or unit logbooks. I think for our purposes today, without discussing things in previous trials, all we need to know is that this is one of the books -- you can call it a logbook, you can call it a diary, which was found with the other documents of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia. As to whose handwriting this is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a non-response to your question. I think that we deserve an answer to your question, which is very vital. And it's not up to the witness, albeit he is part of the Prosecution, as we pointed out. It's not up to him to decide what is or did not valid for us today. He should just do his job and answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my question was a very specific one, was without any ambiguity. This specific document, you've had the opportunity to review it. Is it the personal diary of someone? If that's the case, whose personal diary? Apparently Colonel Blaskic's diary? Do you know it or not? So either we have a document that was found in the archives of the HVO in the year 2000, as you've stated, but as far as you're concerned, you have no idea who wrote that document. That could be an answer. Because an expert when faced with a document, especially a handwritten document, would automatically ask himself these types of questions. So I'm not talk here to the staff member of the OTP, I'm talking to the expert who took a solemn declaration and should, as an expert, tell me how he analysed this specific document, how he analysed the way this document was prepared and by whom. What do you have to say to that? And then there is the remaining question of whether this document was drafted by Colonel Blaskic or not. And I'm not asking the question to Mr. Scott. I'm putting the question to you, so don't look at Mr. Scott. Look at me. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is one of the documents which was discovered by us in the archives in Zagreb in 2000. I don't know who the author is other than that it has to be persons working in the centre of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia. I'm also not sure that this document has one single author or multiple authors. I wouldn't characterise it as a personal diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At least your answer is clear. But when I look at the version in B/C/S, I see that I have seven pages in B/C/S. And if I look at the translation in English, it says translation, page 44, page 46, page 47, and so on and so forth. Does that mean that the document has at least 50 pages and that what we have in B/C/S here is only part of the entire document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what that means. This is an excerpt from a longer document, which I believe is a bound notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this notebook, did you read it in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I only read the sections which were relevant for my testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you see it in its -- did you see the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the originals of this and other books in the archives in Zagreb in either the summer or fall of 2000. And I remember particularly well, because at the time there was a great deal of controversy as to where the diaries of General Blaskic were, and when we found these -- I remember finding these particular volumes and having these particular volumes copied at that time, because at the time it was very significant for the Kordic trial, which was then in its Defence phase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must confess I'm a bit amazed that we do not at least have a photocopy of the cover or the first page, which normally has some sort of indication on the source, and perhaps the very last page where sometimes there is a signature. How come that we do not have this? Is this out of your control or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- that would be the fault of the Prosecution team and the not the fault of Mr. Tomljanovich. He did not prepare these particular exhibits. So if fault -- if there is fault, then the fault lies not with Mr. Tomljanovich but with the team. As I indicated about ten minutes ago, this is indeed an excerpt from a much longer document, and we will be happy to provide -- in fact, I've already requested, I've already requested that the full document be made available, be investigated and made available. Excuse me. I think I have the floor at the moment on this, and I want to be heard just as other counsel want to be heard as well. This witness was asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the entire document, you've disclosed it to the Defence probably. So the Defence has had the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't say that while I'm standing here right now. If anyone thinks -- if anyone in the courtroom thinks that I would have 9.000 documents under exact disclosure committed to memory, I'm sorry, you're mistaken. I'm very happy to make further inquiries if the Chamber gives me a chance to do so. But no, I do not have all the information in my head as I stand here this moment. I'm happy to answer the Judges' inquiries, any inquires you'd like to direct to us given the opportunity to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, two things. First of all, bearing in mine the response of the expert witness, without reference to what my learned friend has said, I propose that examination on this document be suspended and that counsel moves on, because the witness only knows that the document was found in the archives of Croatia, and this fact alone does not make the document acceptable per se or describe it per se. Secondly, Your Honours, at the end of the excerpt we have there is a clause about the number of sheets of paper, and it states clearly: "This notebook contains a hundred." It's written out and also in figures, "a hundred marked sheets and will be used for keeping the war diary." And it's signed by the commander of the operative zone of Central Bosnia, Tihomir Blaskic, printed out and then signed by him, or at least it appears to be signed by him. So first of all there are a hundred pages, and we've been dealing with two or three. Secondly, he states clearly that the notebook containing a hundred pages will in the future be used for keeping a war diary. So this is the basis for something that occurred later. I propose that this document be excluded and that we move on, but I have to reiterate we were not given notice that the witness would be entering into this domain. So in my view, this whole area of examination should be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll conclude a discussion on this point. Mr. Scott, the Defence of General Praljak tells us that the witness statement, if he had the opportunity to view this document is however not in a position to tell us who prepared this document, who is the author of the document, and based on that the Defence of General Praljak would like the document to be excluded. What do you have to answer? And then they'll move on to another topic. Of course, the Chamber will make a ruling afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, these questions are taking us in circles and they do not go to the reliability or accuracy of this document or to the work of this witness. First of all, I don't know how many times -- more times I need to say what I said about 15 minutes ago. This is an excerpt of a longer document. Now, the Prosecution, frankly, feels a bit whipsawed on this because on the one hand we're told every day that there's too many documents and too many pages. Just this day - just this day - I was asked by court staff to select only the relevant pages of a longer document. When I do that I'm acting in compliance with the instructions, and then I'm criticised for not giving you another 200, 400 pages. So I'm happy to do that, but at some point I represented from the outset, I think -- I'll be happy to go back to the first transcript reference, which is now probably about 20 minutes ago. As I said, this is an excerpt of a much longer document, and I also indicated I do not have all the details concerning the document committed to memory. I will be happy to provide the Chamber with that additional information if I have it. Secondly, secondly, if I can put questions to this witness about the documents and others like it, I think it's -- I think it can be fairly addressed. When an historian goes into an archive there is a vast array of material that's available. It has the indicia of reliability up to -- it's in the official state archive. It bears an archival stamp. It may be consistent with other information known to the -- to the researcher, and there's all sorts of reasons why this document and reliance on the document may be perfectly acceptable and the kind of work that historians and researchers do every day. And the attention that's been put on this document, the criticisms that have been put on this document the last 20 minutes or so is -- is not reasonable to beyond a certain point. And I agree we will provide the Chamber with additional such information that we have, but I submit, Your Honour, that much of this has been blown entirely out of proportion simply for the purposes of obstructing this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only questions -- question that was of interest to the Judges was the source of the document, and you've told us about it. You've told us that this document was discovered in the archives in Zagreb. Now, about the reliability. Yes, if we asked the question about the source of the document, it's because of Mr. Praljak's comments, who said that he did not recognise what he was supposed to have said during that meeting. So when reviewing the reliability of the document, we decided to inquire about the provenance of the document. We haven't made a definite ruling. We'll have -- might have questions put to the witness about that during the cross-examination. Mr. Kovacic might give us additional information. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me if I'm trying the Chamber's patience. I don't mean to. But this is another perfect example of -- with all respect, Mr. Praljak shouldn't be allowed to get up and pop up and give testimony during the testimony of another witness. He stands up and says I don't agree. I don't know what that document was about. I don't remember. This is not what I said. Well, if he wants to put on his case and Mr. Praljak wants to take the witness stand some time, he can say that. He can call witness to that effect, and then that witness will also, just as here, be subject to cross-examination. That but -- for just -- just standing up and doing this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, that was not the issue. We have an expert witness who is testifying, and who in line of -- as part of a line of questions is telling us that there was a meeting between General Praljak and various brigade commanders. The expert witness tells us about what General Praljak said about a number of issues. Mr. Praljak, who is the main person concerned, said, "I was present at that meeting but I don't recognise my statements." So automatically the Judges react by saying, "Where does that document come from?" We can see this is a handwritten document. I think these are legitimate questions that the Judges are entitled to ask. It does not mean that this document is irrelevant or has no probative value, not at you will. We'll make that determination at the end. We are in the middle of this process. We have not completed if. We are now going to move on to another topic. I see that Mr. Karnavas wants to stand up, but if that's about the same issue, I don't really see the point of giving you the floor, but, yes, if you really want to speak, I'll give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to supplement a little bit here, because first of all, nobody is questioning the integrity of the Prosecution. We are questioning the integrity of the document itself, just as the Prosecution, in the Blaskic case, or now they're reopening the Blaskic case and they're making accusations particularly against one of the counsel, Defence counsel, of having forged documents, presented those documents to the Tribunal. That's why the sensitivity -- there's a high -- we're highly sensitive about these sorts of documents. We want to know not just where they came from and simply because a document came from an archive does not necessarily mean that a document is authentic, especially when the Prosecution is claiming, and I assume they have a basis for making claims, that documents forged and put into the official archives. These are their allegations that they're making. And these are relevant documents. So that's why -- and this gentleman, apparently, is involved in all these cases. So he should know the documents. That's why we're -- we're challenging all of this. And we believe that in all these documents there should be a foundation by this particular gentleman. Where did he get the document, if he knows how it was generated, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No. We'll stop here, because we could discuss the matter for days. We'll now move on to another topic. If you wish to do so, if you wish to use your time that way during the cross-examination, you will be in a position to ask further questions to the witness about that topic during cross-examination but we'll now move on to something else because we've now spent 20 times discussing this topic. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said I would if given the time to get more information before we leave, the entire document -- I am told and I verified it in e-court myself, the entire document is Exhibit P 01796. It is fully translated, and it had been disclosed to the Defence at least since the 11th of February, 2005. If I could ask that the witness please be shown document P 01789.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a record from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone of the HVO dated, on the second page, indicating a stamp date of 2 April, 1993, a report by the -- apparently the duty officer Franjo Sliskovic. Can I ask you please to look at the second page, item number 2. If you can go up higher on the page. Well, that's not the translation that I'm looking at. Perhaps the previous page in that version then, please. Go to the bottom of that page. Does that record of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone corroborate that there was a meeting with General Praljak at this time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, as Mr. Praljak has just confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you next to go, please, to P 02124. And can you tell us what this is and how this relates to the other documents we've talked about today.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter from Jadranko Prlic dated the 27th of April, 1993, and it's written to the municipal governments of Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, and Travnik, all of which are in this part of Central Bosnia which was -- we've been talking about with the last few documents and which was in the area of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. And Mr. Prlic is informing them that the HVO HZ HB held a meeting on the 24th of April, three days earlier, related to these problems and the conflicts between the Muslims and the Croats there, and he announces his attention to -- or their intention to send a working group made up of vice-president of the HVO HZ HB, Kresimir Zubak, the head of the justice department Zoran Buntic and the head of the subdepartment for social welfare and the family Ilija Zuljevic. And to study the situation and propose measures to be taken. And he reminds them that "It is necessary to prevent facts and the situation to the working group and ensure the conditions for the realisation of this task." And it's related to the previous documents in that. It's his taking -- it's the actions of Mr. Prlic and the HVO HZ HB in regards to some of these incidents that had followed the 16th of April when fighting had broken out in this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I ask you please next to look at Exhibit P 02142. And can you tell us what this document is and what it is about, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report on a meeting which was held in Citluk, which is just very close to Mostar, on the 29th of April, 1993, and it's called a meeting of the HZ HB, and we should be careful. As far as I can tell from this document, this is not per se a meeting of the Presidency of the HZ HB but a meeting of members of the Presidency of the HZ HB as well as the members of the -- here it's called the government of the HZ HB HVO, and this is another example of what I talked about yesterday, that the HZ HB HVO can colloquially be called the government, as well as other Croat dignitaries, municipal presidents, and HDZ municipal chiefs. Altogether, about 60 persons, and they're discussing the current political and military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall the particular reasons request this meeting was organised and called around the 29th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because there was a great deal of fighting in Central Bosnia between the ABiH and the HVO at this time. This was a serious situation and that's why this meeting was called, I'm sure. It doesn't say explicitly but it's called -- here it's explicitly stated for information about the joint statement with Mr. Izetbegovic as well as the political and military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as we look forward into this document does it again follow a format of giving a summary, a report, it's not verbatim, but a form of minutes as to what different participants in the meeting said?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would call these minutes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 of the document, for example, about the middle of the page are there comments or statements attributed to Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are. And Mr. Stojic says -- and before I read the quote I'll just mention that this is in regards to the joint statement or alleged joint statement between Izetbegovic and Boban. He says: "All reports from the field indicate that the Muslims have not accepted the statement. They are attacking Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Konjic, et cetera. They are carrying out ethnic cleansing. The Croats have been driven out from Travnik even though the town is being held under siege. I ask for a political decision ordering units to advance into that part of the HZ HB."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the bottom of that same page there's a comment or intervention attributed to Mr. Zubak. Can you look at that entry and again does it tie back into other documents and information that we discussed this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zubak here, I assume this is a typo as far as Brnetic, but he says that he visited Zenica, Busovaca, and Vitez, as was mentioned in the earlier document by -- written by Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go on to the next page there is some discussion by someone by the name of Anto Valenta, which I'm not sure the Chamber has heard about before perhaps. I may be wrong. Can you tell who Mr. Valenta was and the position he held as of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my report, I mention that after the first wave of appointments to the HVO HZ HB, the appointments -- the persons appointed were overwhelmingly from Herzegovina. Thereafter, three vice-presidents were appointed from areas outside of Herzegovina to represent areas outside of Herzegovina, and one of these persons, who was a vice-president of the HZ HB HVO, was Anto Valenta, who, prior to the war, was a schoolteacher, I believe in Vitez. And he published a book shortly before the war advocating the relocation of populations in Bosnia so that the Croats would occupy one section solely, the Bosnians would occupy a middle section solely, and the Serbs another section solely, and to solve political problems through ethnic resettlement, which was what he was most famous for before becoming president of the HZ HB HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then directing your attention, please, to the last page of the minutes and the final statements attributed to Mr. Boban. There is this language in item number 2 under those comments: "In making a decision, certain limiting factors must be taken into account, especially when it concerns the Republic of Croatia. Due to the events in Vitez (the village of Ahmici), EU ministers have almost announced sanctions against Croatia." In reference to the language that says "certain limiting factors," can you provide any assistance to the Chamber as to, based on your investigation, inquiry, what that reference would be about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think in the context, especially since he mentions problems like Ahmici and mentions sanctions against Croatia, the warning is that the HVO HZ HB or Herceg-Bosna in general would need to certainly watch its behaviour and its image with the international community, because any trouble the international community -- or any trouble the Republic of Croatia has with the international community is a problem at the same time for Herceg-Bosna, and the Republic of Croatia would be held accountable for the actions of persons in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the witness be asked what that interpretation is based upon, whether it's simply a matter of speculation or whether there's actually any substance for it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please go ahead and provide the answer.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't include the evidence that was based upon because that evidence is mainly evidence from the transcripts which were made in the office of President Franjo Tudjman. It was not the intent of this report to discuss these issues or to address those documents. However, the subject of international sanctions being levelled against Croatia because of the behaviour of Herceg-Bosna was discussed quite a few times and was quite an important worry for the Croatian government during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I ask you now to go to Exhibit 21 -- P -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for you to ask the question, but you didn't. So I'm going to ask it. In this document, I can see that the document was prepared by two persons, Pero Krizanac and Drago Bilandzija, but I can also see mention made of annexed papers or enclosures that is to say joint statements of Boban and Izetbegovic, and the conclusions of the meeting. Now, the conclusions, we don't seem to have them. So, Mr. Expert, was your attention drawn to that, because there was supposed to be some conclusions because we can see the interventions of various people but then we see conclusions. Have you seen those conclusions or not? Never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have seen these conclusions and I cite -- they are a separate exhibit and a separate document, and I do cite them in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you have the references?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was the next exhibit I was going to go to, P 02198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- may I before we go that way have an answer to a question of detail? The second person to have prepared the report, Mr. Bilandzija, is defined as "head." Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Bilandzija was the head of, to be honest. It might -- no, I'm sorry, I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go then to Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an observation on my part. As you just said, apparently the conclusions are in the following document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But looking at the document and the typing and so on, I can see that it's -- it wasn't typed on the same machine, typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not saying it was the same -- I'm not saying it was the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Taking -- taking that up, it is also from Vakuf and from the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps the witness can explain these items if given the opportunity to do so. I did not suggest that it is the same document. Your Honour, Mr. President, asked if there was a record of conclusions. This is a record of the conclusions of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is that it's not the same document. But I can see in the previous document that there should be some conclusions, and you said the conclusions are in the document numbered 2198.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now you're saying yes, but perhaps it's not the same document or the same conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that's what I'm querying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My statement in the transcript will show that I never said it was the same document. I said the conclusions of the meeting were reflected in a document, and I submit to the Court that they are submit -- that they are reflected among -- perhaps among other places in Exhibit P 02198. But perhaps if we could put questions to the witness, the witness will be able to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have Exhibit P 02198 available to you, can you look at that document and can you assist the Chamber with whether the conclusions of the Citluk meeting are stated in this document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, the first page of this document is the cover letter to the contents. It's being forwarded later. It's being forwarded by Ivan Saric, chairman of the HDZ from Uskoplje. It's the same town as Gornji Vakuf. Uskoplje is just the non-Muslim sounding name for Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who gave Gornji Vakuf the name of Uskoplje?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used during the war. The Herceg-Bosna officials changed the name of a number of towns. Gornji Vakuf became Uskoplje. Prozor -- let's see here. Yeah. Prozor became Rama. A few others. They referred to Tuzla solely --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll stop for a moment because Judges are engaged in a separate conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you were on your feet. If you want to challenge it, you can challenge it during the cross-examination. That's the proper time to do that. Otherwise, we stop the proceedings. Continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. By way of that introduction, then, sir, can you then take us to the document and make any comments that you would in response to the questions that have been raised by some of the Judges in the last few minutes about these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, the cover letter says that he's forwarding two different things. First of all, minutes of a meeting held in the Presidency in Travnik is one thing, and the second thing is the conclusions of the top representatives of Croat people who met in Citluk. And what follows, then, he is sending it to Pavo Mlakic, what follows then on the next page are the conclusions of the meeting, and there's all together 11 of them and it's entitled, "Meeting of the highest Croat representatives in Citluk."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Have you seen any other accounts of giving -- stating the conclusions of this meeting in Citluk, either in the media or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. Which doesn't mean that there aren't any, but I have not seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The -- in the first page of the document, the report, the enclosure, not the cover letter, after a long -- it says: "After a long-lasting discussion which among others who participated, Mr. Boban ..." and others, in that list of names there is the name Miro Lasic. I don't know if you're familiar who Mr. Lasic was at that time and what position he held?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you he will it us just very briefly about what position or positions Mr. Lasic held during the time of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. 1993, Mr. Lasic was a member of the BiH Presidency, and I believe, although I'm not sure off the top of my head, but I believe he replaced Stjepan Kljuic in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're talking now about the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going on, then, to the next individual, Mile Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What position -- who was he and what positions did he hoped at this time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic at this particular point in time was still the Prime Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although I don't think he was particularly active in this role at that time. By the end of the year, he would be minister in the HR HB cabinet or interrepublican relations and -- I believe it's called interrepublican relations and foreign relations or some such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But again so there's no confusion, when he's listed here as Prime Minister, and what you've just said a moment ago this is Prime Minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the central government located in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can move on to another topic and set of documents, sir. As part of your report -- let me just see if I can give a page reference. In the area of your report around from about the -- page 88, perhaps, and following, one of the topics that you discuss in your report is a mobilisation that the HVO issued in approximately June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what can you tell us -- just by way of introduction, what you can tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the mobilisation. I think it's the 11th issue of Narodni List for that year. I don't believe it's in this part of my -- I don't believe it's in this part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the one that you mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the one I mentioned yesterday in which -- signed by both Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic ordering mobilisation and, among other things, ordering persons to show up at their local -- or to show up at defence offices for the mobilisation. I think it also mentions a curfew and other items.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness be shown P 02707.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the order. Or the decision on carrying out mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, I believe, and can you correct me if I'm wrong, that there was something different about the publication of this particular decision in the Narodni List, the timing of it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned yesterday, generally speaking the Narodni List would come out periodically when there was enough material to fill an entire issue. However, this is the only instance in which a whole issue was one order or one decision and issued immediately by itself as an entire issue of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I then ask you to go, please, to Exhibit P 03038. As soon as you have that --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a document signed by both Bruno Stojic and Jadranko Prlic on the 30th of June, 1993, which -- it is a public appeal following the attack by the ABiH on the -- I think it's on the northern barracks in Mostar, and it's an appeal to the public, a sort of call to arms, a rally. 12

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I just ask you, in terms of the issue of mobilisation, can I just ask you to look at item number 1 on the bottom of the first page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can just confirm to the Judges whether this document also relates to the issue of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and it states -- before you get to the actual numbers, it makes it clear that -- that this order is being issued by Bruno Stojic in particular, and the first order is for all conscripts to report to their units in the next 24 hours. And then there's a number of other parts to this which include the curfew and closing of shops and catering facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, whether this order was put into effect?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was. I believe it went further down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could then look at Exhibit P 03077.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a question that I all -- have already asked another witness, but since you are an expert witness here I'd like to hear you point of view. In the B/C/S document, this famous 3083 document, it says "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," as a heading, and underneath the "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now, the fact that it mentions the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an expert what conclusions can you make from that? What do you deduce from that? What was the reason for the fact that the community of Herceg-Bosna also put Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas there was a Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? So what can you tell us as an expert on this very minor point but, nevertheless, interesting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I don't think it's necessarily a very minor point, and it is very interesting. On the letterheads of Herceg-Bosna, of the HVO or the HZ HB in that period, beginning about in August of 1992 and beginning through the rest of the HZ HB period, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is put at the top of the letterhead as a sort of pro forma thing. Now, bearing in mind some of the other evidence we've seen, in particular the -- the constitutional court decision nullifying Herceg-Bosna and the basic decisions of Herceg-Bosna, it's a bit surprising to see that. However, keeping in mind the limiting factors which Mr. Boban was discussing in the minutes of the meeting we just saw, one limitation on Herceg-Bosna, I think in this period, and once again I'm basing this on evidence not from -- that I did not use in this report, but a total declaration of independence at this point in time by Herceg-Bosna would have caused serious political troubles for the Republic of Croatia, and that's my speculation. And it's only my speculation. I've never seen an order describing why Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has to appear on the letterhead, but that's what I speculate based on all the evidence I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point in time I -- I must make one observation. The witness made a report and has cited certain documents. If he's going to be offering opinions or speculations, in this instance based on other documents which are not in the report, we need to know exactly what are those documents. It's fine for him to give opinions off the top of his head and say, "Well, we've seen documents," or, "this is from something else I've done, but at least if we're going to double-check this information, we need to know specifically what are those documents. Otherwise, they are just empty opinions based on nothing other than his word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas, but in document P 02142, there is this reference to the limiting factors, and I don't see that the witness has now mentioned any other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't follow His Honour's observation. The point that I'm making is he has indicated in his answer that it's not something that he's put into his report but, rather, from other documents that he's reviewed. That was my understanding, and this is the second time. In fact, I wrote a note to Mr. Murphy to -- cautioning him about when he raised his objection. My whole point is, when he goes off script to -- and give an opinion not included in the report, not referenced in the report, what I am suggesting is he identify what exactly is that material, what is he basing that opinion on. That way we can then cross-examine and or at least you would have the opportunity of reviewing that to make sure that his opinion is based on something that -- other than mere speculation. I don't know if I'm being inarticulate or maybe I'm too tired and I've missed the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am tempted to, but I think it's not my role to argue with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, you can argue any time you wish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you -- I think the last question -- the last question I put to you was to move and whether the mobilisation orders that were look at here, decisions, or calls, whatever you want to call it, calling for that to happen in the letter by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic on the 30th of June, whether that was put into effect, and I just -- I'd just asked you to go to P 03077. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is? And in this instance, I would like you -- anything that ties directly back into the document we were just looking at, please point that out.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is forwarding the previous orders on mobilisation further down to all the battalion commands as well as military police sections and military police administration departments, and it's signed -- I think the signature on the original of this one is actually the signature of Mr. Lavric, who is the deputy of Mr. Coric, but he's signing under Mr. Coric's name, and moving the particulars of Mr. Stojic's order and transmitting it down to subordinates in the military police in regards to mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me to be very specific for a moment. If we can go back to the first page of the English version, whenever we can, and if we look at the order, there's a reference number after the reference to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic, it says "Number 02-1-765/93." And could we -- could I ask that the ushers please take us back to Exhibit 3038. Can you look at the top, the order on this document, sir? Can you confirm to the Judges that the reference number on this document is that number?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reference numbers are identical. It's 02-1-765/93. So this order here, Exhibit 3077, is making direct reference to this earlier order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And does Mr. Coric -- by the order of Mr. Coric, does he put anyone in particular in -- make anyone responsible for the enforcement of these orders?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the second page towards the bottom -- the second page of Mr. Coric's order. If we could have that on the screen. Exhibit 3077. 3077, page 2. Yeah. Oh -- yeah, the second page. Thank you. The paragraph -- scroll up a tiny bit. The paragraph here under the 5th part of the order, it says: "All military police units are charged with the implementation of this order within their zones of responsibility. The unit commanders shall be responsible for the implementation of this order, and checks will be carried out by authorised officers from the military police administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. All right, sir. That completes -- Let me see if I can catch up on exhibits, Mr. President. We tender P 01778; P 01798; P 01796; which is the full version, the long, full version of the Central Bosnia document that we spent so much time talking about; Exhibit P 01788; Exhibit P 01214; Exhibit P 02142; Exhibit P 02198; Exhibit P 03038; and Exhibit P 03077.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I think we have to look at timing. You're running a little late for various reasons. Now, I'm going to ask the registrar to tell me how much time the Prosecution has used thus far, but I think that you have used between five hours and -- five and a quarter hours and five hours, 45 minutes. And we're going to have to take a break anyway in a few minutes' time. You'll have one hour after the break, which will lead us to around 6.00 -- or, rather, you will have used about six hours, and eight hours was what was allotted to you, which means two hours for tomorrow. So I'd like to know how you stand. Where are you at in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour's -- excuse me. Your Honour's observations are on target. In fact our records -- I didn't hear, I didn't have the transcript turned on what the registry computation was. Our calculation, and of course -- of course, the registry's calculation will control, but our calculation is that I have used approximately four hours and 20 minutes of the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They tell me you have used six hours or, rather, five hours and 55 minutes. So that's roughly six hours. So you were given two days, and the two days run out at 7.00. So how much more time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the very least after today I would speculate we would need at least two hours. I would obviously have to sit down and speak with the registry. It may be that the way that Mr. Frejabue was keeping time is not the way the time is being taken now. In the past -- I know that from experience over the last -- since we started trial in April that Ms. Winner's time and the time taken by the registry has almost always been very, very close and there is obviously some reason for that discrepancy which we'll have to explore. I understand that of course we talked about two days. One might have thought that two days we would hopefully get something like seven or eight hours. Now, by my calculations -- if our calculations are correct, then I've only used about half of the time that I had estimated. In any event, I think the Chamber will have seen the interventions and the way that the witness -- I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thought you had not hours but days, and the days were Monday and Tuesday. So in theory, Tuesday runs out at 7.00 p.m., but we'll discuss the matter amongst us Judges. And there were quite a few interventions by the Defence and questions by the Judges, justified, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take the break now anyway. It's half past 5.00, and we reconvene at ten to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Mr. Scott, let me come back to the issue of time. The Judges have discussed the matter. As you know, we had decided to allocate two days to the Prosecution and three days to the Defence. However, we take note of the fact that the Prosecution is running late and will not be in a position to complete direct-examination within two days. So that's why we have decided to add two hours to these original two days. In other words, Mr. Scott, tomorrow you will have two additional hours. Obviously this will have an impact on the time for the Defence. We'll still keep the three days for the Defence, but they will also have two additional hours. Therefore, three days and two hours for the Defence. If you complete on Monday, then that will be very well, but if not, then we will need to postpone the end of the cross-examination to another day, not during the following week but during the week after. So there might be two additional hours on another day, except, of course, if the Defence complete its cross-examination on Monday at 7.00 p.m. Mr. Scott, you have one hour left until 7.00 p.m. today, and you will have two hours tomorrow. I hope that there will be no more interventions and that you'll be able to complete your direct examination within these three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sure Mr. Tomljanovich will enjoy every possible extra hour that he doesn't have to talk to me and cannot talk to me about something else. So we will press on. What I may do, Your Honour, and I just want to be very transparent, is reduce the number of documents that I will put to the witness, recognising that that means that other documents I'll put to the witness will necessarily be in some cases out of context, therefore, I suppose, possibly prompting questions from the Judges as to what's the purpose or context of this document, but I don't have time to go through all the documents, so I'll just jump a bit from document to document, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next turn, sir, to the question of taxes and finance -- strike that. Let me back up. Sir, today so far I have taken you through -- we've covered three essential topics or scenarios, series of events. One was the -- a series of orders related to the 15th of January, 1993, ultimatum. The second scenario or series of events being related to the discussions in early April, 1993 about, again, the subordination of the ABH forces in provinces 3, 8, and 10 to the HVO, and the third scenario I took you through was on the question of mobilisation. In each of those situations I showed you a series of documents. Can you tell the Judges whether -- do those documents illustrate what you saw in your research that the structures and processes that you described generally yesterday, in a general way, were in fact the structures and processes followed in the three scenarios that we went through today?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. As I described yesterday, my report has three parts to it. First describing the foundation documents and the de jure framework, and the second part showing how those structures functioned in practice and how these processes and structures would react and how orders were moved down the line in these situations, de facto, in 1993. Then I returned to the de jure structures of HR HB at the end. But, yes, all of these episodes do show that the system, for the most part, functioned as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next take you to then the topic of taxes and finances. If we can touch on that just for a very few minutes. You included -- that's topics in your report. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown P 00410. And if you have that, sir, can you tell us what that is and again the -- the -- relate it to the parts of your report, if you can help us relate it to the question of taxes and finance in connection with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decree as reprinted in Narodni List from the 28th of August, 1992, and signed by Jadranko Prlic, and it -- it decrees the introduction of a war tax in the territory of the HZ HB in the times of the imminent threat of war, during the state of war, and just very briefly, the tax, as outlined in Article 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hold on one moment, please, because right now we're looking at -- if I can ask the ushers to go to the fourth page of that document because I think there's two different decrees in this exhibit. And for those using a hard copy, looking at a hard copy, it's the fourth page of Exhibit P 00410. Now will you continue, sir now that people have --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Article 2, just very briefly, this tax is described as being a tax of 10 per cent on paid salaries per month. And going on to the next page, it also taxes 3.000 Croatian dinars per month for independently employed entrepreneurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just top you there, sir, because -- in the interest of time.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was one particular tax, but in your report you talk about the various means by which the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the HVO sought to raise revenue or found ways to raise revenue.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one among many ways in which they were raising revenue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you can go back to the first page of that same exhibit, the one we started looking at, and tell us what that decree is about.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- and I'm not sure if that's the same exhibit although the translations are together. That is the decree on opening the account for the budget of the HZ HB, and it establishes a bank account into which the monies for the budget will be deposited. And it was also approved on the same day, 28th of August, 1992, which is soon after the HVO HZ HB began meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you look at Articles 3 and 4 and tell us the purposes or name of the account and where the account, or accounts, was or were, depending if it's single or plural, opened?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Articles 3 and 4 say that the budget account will be opened with the Mostar Public Auditing Service and with the commercial bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this decree was issued by --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's Jadranko Prlic. If we could scroll to the end. He signs the decree. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can next ask you then to turn your attention to Exhibit P 00511. And as soon as you have -- well, let's wait for it to come up on the screen. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the actual request to open that same account for the budget of the HZ HB, and it's dated on the 21st of September, 1992. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And authorises three persons to manage the funds in that particular account with their signatures, the first being Neven Tomic who was the head of the financial department or the finance department, the second Jadranko Prlic the president of the HZ HB HVO, and finally Zeljko Bandic who was an employee of the financial department or finance department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at the -- it's worth in this instance, I think, looking at the B/C/S original, if we could pull up the second page which would be ERN 03424131. Directing your attention, sir, to number 2, can you just go ahead and read that in the original language, allow it to be translated for us, and then indicate whether that then by this document is indicated as Mr. Prlic's signature.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "2. Dr. Jadranko Prlic, president of the HVO HZ HB, who will sign his name as follows." [In English] And then it follows with a signature which I recognise as Mr. Prlic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the other two men have apparently indicated their hand signatures as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next ask you to direct your attention to the last document in all these bundles, which is P 09551. And in the English excerpt, Your Honours, it's going to be -- this document, the way the translations were put together in various bits and pieces, there is not a continuous pagination. So I ask the Chamber to bear with me. If you can go about probably -- approximately four-fifths of the way through the document until you get to the page that says "budget" and item number 1 under that heading it says, "budget revenue." And in the B/C/S document, page 0040 starting at page 5232, the section on finance, starting on page 5232 and continuing on to 0040-5237. And if all else fails, we can put it on the ELMO, I suppose. May I suggest in the interest -- since time is precious, Mr. President, we can just put these two pages on the ELMO, of the English version. I apologise. It will have some yellow markings on it, but I don't think they say a whole lot. First of all, Mr. Tomljanovich, can you remind the Judges what document P 00 -- or, excuse me, P 09551 is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this section here is an excerpt from the whole exhibit, which is the semi-annual report of the HVO for the second half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this report would roughly cover the period from July to December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in this particular section where they actually discuss the budget they cover all of 1993 in certain respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in the beginning here they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your research, Mr. Tomljanovich, did you find that there were accounts given -- accountings given of the budget revenues for 1993 and the expenditures by the HVO in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are, and that's spelled out in this particular document. In the first section we see here, various tax revenues which amount to -- I believe that's 104 billion Croatian dinars. Then there's non-tax revenue in section 2. Revenues from credits in section 3. Donations and other revenues in section 4. Revenues from previous years carried over, and then the total revenue is at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could you go to the next page. Could you put the next page on the ELMO in terms of expenditures?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next page lists the expenditures, and I believe this is all in Croatian dinars. And it lists the various places where the money went in 1993 from January to December, and just a quick look at that you can see that the vast majority of the budget went to the defence department, and the total, it's up here, 169 billion, and total expenditures are 197 billion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. We can go forward. For the record I'm told and I apologise for not having this information at hand previously but pages that were put on the ELMO in the e-court pages are pages 39 and 40 of the English version for the record. In your report, sir, did you also talk about the issues of refugees, handling of prisoners, population movements?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and it's something I spent a great deal of space on, because that was a complicated issue which shows the de facto functioning of the Herceg-Bosna institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. All right. Mr. Tomljanovich, on that point I was going to show you eight documents but because of time I'll only show you two. So if I can direct your attention to P 03052. And as soon as you have Exhibit 3052, P 03052, sorry, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a draft document written by Mr. Berislav Pusic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As Mr. Tomljanovich is also an archival expert, this document is not signed by Mr. Pusic. There is no date and no protocol. So can we hear how the witness knows that the document was actually compiled by Mr. Pusic? I am also interested in the provenance of this document, because I don't see the stamp of the Croatian state archives on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, this document is what we call in our own jargon type signed. That's correct. There is no particular signature from Mr. Berislav Pusic, although this particular document was written most likely right after the foundation of the office for the exchange of prisoners and other persons. This particular document, as far as I remember, is a new document which was provided by the OTP from Bosnian federation authorities, and this was, I believe -- there's two collections we received recently. I believe this collection was the -- either the office for refugees and displaced persons or the collection of the Department for Social Welfare and the Family, although this certainly was not received in the Croatian archives. This was provided to us by Bosnian federation authorities, and it was found in Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, what the document is -- indicates or is about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a proposal for the internal organisation of this office and puts forward the estimation of the funds, equipment, and staff needed, and proposes a flowchart and other details for organising this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me back up and ask you, in your research and in your report, in fact, you cover, among other agencies or bodies, commissions, services related to refugees, prisoner exchanges, et cetera, is one of those bodies something called the Service for Exchange of Prisoners and Other Persons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in particular, did your research show that during this time period, that is approximately mid-1993, going forward, that Mr. Pusic was the head of that office or service?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, his appointment was in Narodni List and that's cited in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And before we leave this document, then, this appears to be at least a proposal over the typed name of Mr. Pusic for the operation of this office?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 03191. And can you tell us -- if you have that, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a translation of the actual appointment signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic on the 5th of July appointing Berislav Pusic head of the service for exchange of prisoners and other persons of the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on your research, Mr. Tomljanovich, can you tell us the title makes reference to "and other persons," who these other persons were?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume, and it's never spelled out explicitly, that "other persons" would be everyone who is not a prisoner of war and would be civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the question of the movement of population, did you also look at the question of Bosnian Croat refugees coming to Herzegovina from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In the summer -- spring and summer of 1993, a great number of Croat refugees arrived in Herzegovina, Western Herzegovina, and other parts of Herceg-Bosna from Central Bosnia and other places after the fighting between the ABiH and the HVO, and they were resettled in various places, but there was a great effort to find places for those refugees, including there in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As part of that, sir, can you tell us, during this time were there ever any discussions or in fact actions to evacuate or move large blocks of population from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina into Herceg-Bosna territory?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was in particular one very large evacuation from Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we get to that, can I ask you to direct your attention to Exhibit P 02283. And can you tell us what that is, and again then relate that back if you will to your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter from Colonel Blaskic, who was the commander of the Central Bosnian military zone, to Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, and Bruno Stojic, and it's in regard to "Your oral order for evacuation of people and the army." And Mr. Blaskic -- or Colonel Blaskic is informing them that the oral order for evacuation which he had received, he's received the order but that he has information on why the order for evacuation will not be taken out -- undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the second paragraph he says that it's not possible because the evacuation would have to be carried out through territories controlled by -- here it says the MOS, which would be really the ABiH, the Bosnian army, and that there's no other way to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he suggests not long after that that they negotiate with the Muslim leadership, and if that's not possible, to negotiate with the persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just stop you briefly. Again, I don't know if the Chamber has seen the reference or the abbreviation "MOS" before, so let me just ask you what is that? An abbreviation for -- literally from the B/C/S language, can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means the Muslim armed forces which is not, as far as I know, not an abbreviation they used for themselves but it was frequently applied in HVO documents to the army of ABiH, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if the ushers could help us by going to the second page of that document. You made reference to the fact that there was some discussion or proposal about approaching the Serbs about being able to evacuate people from Central Bosnia through Serb-controlled territory. Can you point out in the document, that language, to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's in the second sentence on the second page, which is up a little I think. There we are. It's already there. Beginning with "In order to be able to carry out given tasks," this is a quote, "In order to be able to carry out the given tasks, I suggest to openly negotiate on this with the Muslim leadership and in case of their refusal to consider the possibility to pull out across territories controlled -- and in case of their refusal," sorry, I'm going backwards, "to consider the possibility to pull out across territories controlled by the Chetniks, although I am aware that Chetniks are Chetniks and nothing else but Chetniks." By Chetniks here I assume he's using that to refer to the Serbs in general which is not strictly speaking correct or not politically correct, certainly, but that's what he means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to next direct your attention to Exhibit P 03413. And when you look at what document, can you tell us -- first of all tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a letter written on the 13th of July, 1993, to the president -- Presidency of the HZ HB, to the president personally. So it's going personally to Mate Boban. And I believe if you look at the bottom it's signed -- or it's Mr. Prlic at the bottom. If we can look. On behalf of the HVO HZ HB. Yes. It's signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic as president of the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And what is the topic or subject matter of this letter?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. If we could go back to the beginning of the document. Yes. Mr. Prlic is informing -- he's reminding, I believe, and not informing for the first time, he doesn't say that explicitly, but he's informing Mr. Boban of the conclusions reached at an HVO HZ HB meeting on the 15th of June, 1993, and has a number of conclusions which he's telling him about, asking for assistance in various ways, and particular relevant to the earlier documents we saw, Article 3 here, if you see it, says: "A proposal has been put to the Presidency of the HZ HB and Supreme Commander of the HVO to reach the decision to withdraw all military units together with the local Croatian population from areas outside of the defined Croat provinces. For that purpose an assistance of UNPROFOR and UNHCR needs to be requested in the form of an ultimatum."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know whether there were any -- in fact, any evacuations carried out after the 13th of July of 1993? Or movements or withdrawals it's said here.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were a number of evacuations. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I mentioned the one from Vares in particular. Or there were a number of evacuations from Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two other documents two things not dealing with the issue that we're talking about now but before we leave the document in terms of evacuations or movements of people. In Article 2 or paragraph 2 do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Article 2, and this gets back to what we were talking about earlier today, Article 2 reads: "A proposal has been put to the Presidency of the HZ HB and the Supreme Commander of the HVO to urgently seek the military aid for the protection of BiH Croats from the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just go again to then Article 4. Can you tell us anything about what paragraph 4 references, and if you know, whether any steps were taken to --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Indiscernible - overlapping speakers] ... at that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Section number 4 makes reference to a proposal put forward to Mr. Boban to form a wartime cabinet in accordance with a decree on armed forces, which is foreseen in the decree on armed forces. This implies it hadn't actually been done until this period, but later documentation shows that there were smaller meetings of the persons in the cabinet most responsible for these -- for defence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who would -- who would those persons be?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, and off the top of my head Mr. Kvesic as head of the Department of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior some might call it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: MUP.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six of one, half dozen of another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I can go back -- sorry, but before we go to the next item if you go back to paragraph number 3 it says, "... outside of the defined Croat provinces." Now, this document is dated the 13th of July, 1993. Can you assist the Judges in terms of what would be -- if you can, what would be the defined Croat provinces at this time period?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time period actually off the top of my head I'm not sure if the provinces as outlined in Vance-Owen were still on the table or if the maps they were discussing in the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan were already on the table. It would have been one or the other but I'm not sure which at this particular stage. It was late for one and early for another, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
